places.name: Milan Cathedral
places.subtitle: Gothic cathedral · since 1386
places.s30: In front of you stands the heart of Milan. The cathedral is a forest of pink and white marble, crowded with spires, pinnacles and thousands of statues. It took almost six centuries to finish, and it remains one of the most beloved symbols of Italy.
places.m2: Work began in 1386, commissioned by the lord of Milan, Gian Galeazzo Visconti. The marble came from the quarries of Candoglia near Lake Maggiore and travelled on barges along the canals right into the city. The façade was only completed in the nineteenth century at the wish of Napoleon, who had himself crowned King of Italy here in 1805. Ever since, the Milanese say that an endless job is like the building of the Duomo, because the works have never truly stopped. Now look up at the highest spire: up there shines the Madonnina, a gilded copper statue of the Virgin placed in 1774, whom the Milanese regard as their protector. By tradition no building was supposed to rise above her, so when the Pirelli skyscraper did, a small copy of the statue was set on its roof. Look also at the gargoyles jutting from the walls: fantastic creatures that carry rainwater away. If you like, you can climb to the terraces and walk among the spires, almost face to face with the Madonnina.
places.look: Look at the top of the highest spire: the golden Madonnina.
places.aliases: Catedral de Milán | Cathédrale de Milan | Duomo di Milano | Mailänder Dom | Milan Cathedral

places.name: Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II
places.subtitle: Iron and glass arcade · 1877
places.s30: You are walking into Milan's drawing room. This covered arcade links Piazza del Duomo with Piazza della Scala, a cross of streets beneath a vault of iron and glass. Historic cafés, elegant shops and visitors from everywhere have filled it for more than a century and a half.
places.m2: The design was entrusted to the architect Giuseppe Mengoni, and the main works took place between 1865 and 1877. The arcade celebrated a newly unified Italy and bears the name of its first king. Its story has a bitter ending, though: at the end of 1877, on the eve of the inauguration of the entrance arch, Mengoni died after falling from the scaffolding. Now walk to the centre, where the two arms cross to form a great octagon under a glass dome. Look down at the floor: the mosaics show the coats of arms of Milan, Turin, Florence and Rome. The arms of Turin feature a bull, and tradition says that spinning around with your heel on its private parts brings good luck. The ritual is so popular that the mosaic wears away and has to be restored from time to time. Then look up at the lunettes beneath the dome, decorated with allegories of the continents. Milanese and travellers have met here for generations, and it is the perfect spot for a break.
places.look: Look at the floor in the centre: Turin's bull and the hole worn by heels.
places.aliases: Galerie Victor-Emmanuel II | Galería Víctor Manuel II | Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II

places.name: La Scala Opera House
places.subtitle: Opera house · since 1778
places.s30: In front of you is one of the most famous opera houses in the world. Its façade is sober, almost modest, yet masterpieces by Verdi and Puccini had their premieres inside. In the middle of the square, Leonardo da Vinci watches you from his pedestal.
places.m2: The theatre was designed by Giuseppe Piermarini after a fire destroyed the old court theatre, and it opened in 1778. Its name comes from the church that stood here before, Santa Maria alla Scala, founded by Regina della Scala, wife of Bernabò Visconti. Verdi's Nabucco and Otello and Puccini's Madama Butterfly and Turandot all had their world premieres on this stage. Bombs in 1943 badly damaged the building, and the reopening in 1946 was entrusted to Arturo Toscanini. Even today the season opens on the seventh of December, the feast of Saint Ambrose, the city's patron. Inside there is also the Theatre Museum, with costumes, instruments and portraits. Now turn towards the centre of the square: the statue of Leonardo, made by Pietro Magni in 1872, is surrounded by four of his pupils. The Milanese jokingly call it a litre in four, because it looks like a bottle with four glasses around it. Finally, facing the theatre stands Palazzo Marino, the city hall.
places.look: Look at the base of Leonardo's statue: four pupils stand around him.
places.aliases: La Scala Opera House | Mailänder Scala | Teatro alla Scala | Teatro de La Scala | Théâtre de la Scala

places.name: Royal Palace of Milan
places.subtitle: Neoclassical palace · Piermarini, 1778
places.s30: Beside the cathedral, with its pale façade opening onto a small square, stands the palace from which Milan was governed for centuries. Lords, dukes, governors and kings all lived here. Today it is one of the great exhibition venues of the city.
places.m2: In the Middle Ages this was the site of the Broletto Vecchio, the seat of city government. Then came the Visconti and the Sforza, who turned it into a court residence. What you see today is the work of Giuseppe Piermarini, the architect of La Scala, who between 1773 and 1778 gave the palace this sober, elegant neoclassical façade for the Habsburgs. Notice how the façade steps back from the square to form the Piazzetta Reale, almost a courtyard open to the city. A musical curiosity: the palace once held a court theatre, where in 1770 a Mozart only fourteen years old presented his opera Mitridate. That theatre burned down a few years later, and La Scala was built to replace it. In 1943 bombing devastated the Hall of the Caryatids, which still bears the marks of the fire. It was right there, in 1953, that Picasso's Guernica was exhibited, in a hall wounded by war just like the Spanish town in the painting. Today the palace hosts major exhibitions and, in one wing, the Duomo Museum.
places.look: Look how the façade steps back to embrace the Piazzetta Reale.
places.aliases: Palacio Real de Milán | Palais royal de Milan | Palazzo Reale | Royal Palace of Milan

places.name: Piazza dei Mercanti
places.subtitle: Medieval square · 1233
places.s30: Just a few steps from the cathedral, you enter the heart of medieval Milan. This intimate square was the centre of civic life: justice was administered here, votes were cast and trade was done. In the middle stands the Palazzo della Ragione with its arcaded portico.
places.m2: The Palazzo della Ragione, also called the Broletto Nuovo, was built between 1228 and 1233. On the ground floor the great portico sheltered merchants and their stalls, while upstairs the judges and the city council met. The top floor, with its oval windows, was added in 1773. On the side of the palace facing the square, look for the relief of the chief magistrate Oldrado da Tresseno on horseback. Then search among the arches of the portico for a small and very old carving: the scrofa semilanuta, a sow covered in wool on only half of its body. According to an ancient legend, the name Mediolanum comes from here, from medio lanum, half wool. Opposite you is the Loggia degli Osii, in black and white marble, built in 1316 for Matteo Visconti: sentences were proclaimed from its balcony. Next to it stands the Palazzo delle Scuole Palatine, with a statue of Saint Augustine on its façade, and in the middle of the square there is an old well.
places.look: Look along the portico arches: find the little half woolly sow.
places.aliases: Piazza dei Mercanti | Place des Marchands | Plaza de los Mercaderes

places.name: Museo del Novecento
places.subtitle: Twentieth century art museum · since 2010
places.s30: In front of you, on the edge of the square, stands the Arengario, a pale stone building with long arcades. Since 2010 it has housed the Museo del Novecento, devoted to Italian art of the last century. In the evening, a winding neon line lights up behind the upper window.
places.m2: The Arengario was designed in the 1930s by a group of architects including Piero Portaluppi and Giovanni Muzio, and work began in 1937. The war halted construction, and the building was only finished after the conflict. Its name recalls the arengo, the ancient assembly of citizens. On the façade, look for the reliefs carved by Arturo Martini, which tell the story of Milan. In 2010 the building was turned into a museum to a design by Italo Rota, with a spiral ramp rising from the entrance. Inside you will find the Futurists, led by Boccioni, followed by Modigliani, de Chirico, Morandi and a room devoted to Lucio Fontana. The view of the cathedral from the top floor is one of the finest in the city, and from up there the spires seem almost within reach. Now raise your eyes to the highest window: that luminous tangle is a neon sculpture by Fontana, created in 1951 and visible from the square as well, especially once darkness falls.
places.look: Look at the top window: Lucio Fontana's tangle of neon light.
places.aliases: Museo del Novecento | Musée du Novecento

places.name: San Bernardino alle Ossa
places.subtitle: Church and ossuary · thirteenth century
places.s30: This quiet looking church beside the basilica of Santo Stefano hides one of the most surprising places in Milan. Inside there is a small chapel whose walls are entirely covered with human skulls and bones, carefully arranged as decoration. Unsettling and fascinating at the same time.
places.m2: It all begins in the thirteenth century, when a cemetery next to the nearby hospital filled up and a room was built to gather the bones. A few decades later a church was added beside it. Over the centuries the building suffered collapses and, in the early eighteenth century, a serious fire, and it was rebuilt by the architect Carlo Giuseppe Merlo. Today it bears the name of Saint Bernardino of Siena. The bones do not belong to martyrs, as people long believed, but mostly to hospital patients, condemned prisoners and clergy buried in the area. Inside, the ossuary is astonishing: skulls set into niches, along the cornices, on the pillars and around the doors, arranged in decorative patterns. Look up and the contrast is complete: the vault was frescoed by Sebastiano Ricci in 1695 with a triumph of souls among angels. A popular legend says that on the night of the dead, the second of November, the skeleton of a little girl comes back to life and leads the others in a dance.
places.look: Look at the plain façade: nothing hints at the chapel of bones within.
places.aliases: San Bernardino alle Ossa

places.itwiki: Chiesa di Santa Maria presso San Satiro
places.name: Santa Maria presso San Satiro
places.subtitle: Renaissance church · Bramante, 1482
places.s30: This church, almost hidden among the buildings of Via Torino, holds one of the most famous optical illusions in the history of art. Donato Bramante had no room for a real choir, so he created a fake one, so convincing that from the entrance it seems several metres deep.
places.m2: On this spot, in 879, Archbishop Anspertus built a small chapel dedicated to Saint Satyrus, the brother of Saint Ambrose. The Romanesque brick bell tower beside it dates from the eleventh century and is among the oldest in Milan. In the fifteenth century a new church was planned to house an image of the Virgin believed to be miraculous, and the project was entrusted to Bramante. There was one problem: a street ran right behind the altar, leaving no room for a choir. So Bramante came up with a brilliant solution: in a depth of less than one metre, using stucco and painted perspective, he created the illusion of a deep apse with coffered vaults and pillars. Once inside, look at it from the back of the nave, then walk up to it from the side: the trick suddenly gives itself away. The small ancient chapel, now known as the Chapel of the Pietà, still stands beside the church. The façade you see from the street, on the other hand, was only completed in the nineteenth century.
places.look: Look at the Romanesque brick bell tower, one of the oldest in Milan.
places.aliases: Santa Maria presso San Satiro

places.name: Sforza Castle
places.subtitle: Home of the Sforza dukes · from 1450
places.s30: In front of you stands Sforza Castle, the great fortress of the lords of Milan. Francesco Sforza rebuilt it from 1450 as his princely home. The tall central tower is the Filarete Tower, the castle's symbol and its gateway towards the city.
places.m2: The first castle was built by the Visconti family in the fourteenth century, straddling the city walls. When the last Visconti died in 1447, the Milanese partly tore it down, and in 1450 Francesco Sforza brought it back to life as a palace. At the court of his son Ludovico il Moro worked Bramante and Leonardo da Vinci, who painted the vault of the Sala delle Asse as a bower of intertwined trees. Centuries of foreign rule followed and the castle became a barracks. By the late nineteenth century some even proposed demolishing it, until the architect Luca Beltrami saved it with a thorough restoration. The tower in front of you, designed by Filarete, blew up in 1521 because of the gunpowder stored inside. Beltrami rebuilt it from old drawings and opened it in 1905, dedicated to King Umberto the First. Look up: in a niche on the tower stands Saint Ambrose, the city's patron. Inside the walls today are the Castle Museums, home to Michelangelo's very last sculpture, the Rondanini Pietà.
places.look: Look at the niche on the Filarete Tower: Saint Ambrose, patron of Milan.
places.aliases: Castello Sforzesco | Castillo Sforzesco | Château des Sforza | Sforza Castle

places.name: Sempione Park
places.subtitle: English landscape park · late 1800s
places.s30: You are in Sempione Park, the great green lung behind the castle. This was once the hunting ground of the Sforza dukes and later a military parade ground. In the late nineteenth century it became an English garden, with lawns, a pond and avenues reaching the Arch of Peace.
places.m2: The park was designed by the architect Emilio Alemagna, who imagined an English landscape of gentle hills, clumps of trees and a winding pond, and opened it to the Milanese in the late nineteenth century. All around the lawns, pieces of the city's history survive. The Arena Civica, built in Napoleon's time, hosted chariot races and even mock naval battles, flooding the field with water. The Palazzo dell'Arte, home of the Triennale design museum, dates from the 1930s, and next to it rises the Branca Tower, the metal tower Gio Ponti designed in 1933. Near the pond, look for a small iron bridge with four little mermaids: the Bridge of the Little Mermaids, one of the first cast iron bridges in Italy. It once crossed the Naviglio canal in Via San Damiano and was moved here when the canal was covered over in the 1930s. The Milanese still jokingly call it the bridge of the Ghisini sisters. On the edge of the park stands the Civic Aquarium, an elegant Art Nouveau building from 1906.
places.look: Look for the Branca Tower, Gio Ponti's metal tower over a hundred metres tall.
places.aliases: Parc Sempione | Parco Sempione | Parque Sempione | Sempione Park

places.name: Arch of Peace
places.subtitle: Neoclassical triumphal arch · 1807-1838
places.s30: In front of you is the Arch of Peace, the marble triumphal arch that opens the Simplon road towards France. Napoleon wanted it, the Austrians finished it, and today it closes Sempione Park on the side opposite the castle.
places.m2: The arch was begun in 1807 to a design by Luigi Cagnola, celebrating Napoleon's victories right at the start of the new Simplon road, which crossed the Alps all the way to Paris. When the emperor fell, work stopped, and it was the Austrians who resumed it, dedicating the monument to the peace reached in Europe in 1815. It was inaugurated in 1838. Look up at the top: the bronze chariot drawn by six horses is the Sestiga della Pace, the work of the sculptor Abbondio Sangiorgio. The story goes that the Austrians had it face the city, so that the horses would turn their backs on France. In June 1859, after the victory at Magenta, Napoleon the Third and Victor Emmanuel the Second rode into Milan beneath this arch, and the inscriptions were rewritten to celebrate independence. On either side of the arch you will notice two small neoclassical buildings: these were the customs houses, where duties were paid on goods entering the city.
places.look: Look at the top of the arch: a bronze chariot pulled by six horses.
places.aliases: Arc de la Paix | Arch of Peace | Arco de la Paz | Arco della Pace | Friedensbogen

places.name: Brera Palace and Art Gallery
places.subtitle: Baroque palace and art gallery · since 1809
places.s30: In front of you is the Brera Palace, built as a Jesuit college in the seventeenth century. Today it is a small city of learning, home to the Academy of Fine Arts, a great library, an astronomical observatory, a botanical garden and one of Italy's finest art galleries.
places.m2: The name Brera comes from braida, an old word for a grassy field on the edge of town. A convent of the Humiliati order stood here, then the Jesuits arrived and from 1615 had this palace built to a design by Francesco Maria Richini. When the order was suppressed, Empress Maria Theresa of Austria turned it into a centre of culture: the Academy of Fine Arts, the Braidense Library and the botanical garden were founded, alongside the observatory the Jesuits had already established. The art gallery was born under Napoleon and opened in 1809, gathering paintings taken from suppressed churches and convents. Today it holds masterpieces such as Mantegna's Dead Christ, Raphael's Marriage of the Virgin and Hayez's The Kiss. Step into the main courtyard, with its double tier of columned arcades, and look at the centre: the bronze statue is Napoleon, naked, as Mars the Peacemaker, cast from a model by Antonio Canova. From the courtyard a grand staircase leads up to the museum.
places.look: Look at the centre of the courtyard: a bronze Napoleon, after Canova's model.
places.aliases: Brera Palace and Art Gallery | Palacio y Pinacoteca de Brera | Palais et pinacothèque de Brera | Palazzo di Brera e Pinacoteca | Palazzo di Brera und Pinacoteca

places.name: Ambrosian Library and Art Gallery
places.subtitle: Library and art gallery · since 1609
places.s30: In front of you is the Ambrosiana, founded by Cardinal Federico Borromeo in the early seventeenth century. It was one of the first libraries in Europe open to the public, and beside the books the cardinal added an art gallery, believing that art should educate.
places.m2: The library opened its doors in 1609 and takes its name from Saint Ambrose, patron of Milan. Federico Borromeo, cousin of Saint Charles Borromeo, sent his agents across Europe and the East to hunt for manuscripts, and in 1618 he also donated his collection of paintings, which became the art gallery. Here you will find the Codex Atlanticus, the largest collection of Leonardo da Vinci's pages, together with his Portrait of a Musician. The rooms also hold Caravaggio's Basket of Fruit and Raphael's huge preparatory cartoon for The School of Athens. A true curiosity: one of the library's prefects was Achille Ratti, who in 1922 became Pope Pius the Eleventh, which is why the square at the entrance bears his name. Then look behind the building, towards Piazza San Sepolcro: according to scholars, this is where the forum of Roman Milan lay, the heart of the ancient city.
places.look: Look at the square next door: San Sepolcro stands where the Roman forum was.
places.aliases: Ambrosian Library and Art Gallery | Biblioteca e Pinacoteca Ambrosiana | Biblioteca und Pinacoteca Ambrosiana | Biblioteca y Pinacoteca Ambrosiana | Bibliothèque et pinacothèque Ambrosienne

places.name: Basilica of San Marco
places.subtitle: Augustinian church · from 1254
places.s30: In front of you is the Basilica of San Marco, in the heart of Brera. Built by the Augustinians in the thirteenth century, it is one of the largest churches in Milan after the cathedral. Young Mozart stayed here, and Verdi conducted the premiere of his Requiem here.
places.m2: Tradition links the church's name to Venice, as thanks for the help the Venetians gave the Milanese against Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. The Gothic church was built by the Augustinians from 1254, and in the seventeenth century the interior was remodelled in Baroque style. The facade you see, however, comes from the Gothic Revival restoration by Carlo Maciachini in 1871. Look at the marble portal, the rose window and the mosaic in the lunette above the entrance, then raise your eyes to the bell tower, which dates back to the fourteenth century. In early 1770 the very young Mozart lived for a few months in the convent next door, during his first journey to Italy with his father Leopold. And on 22 May 1874, the first anniversary of Alessandro Manzoni's death, Giuseppe Verdi conducted the first performance of his Messa da Requiem right here, written in honour of the great writer. Inside, fourteenth century frescoes and sarcophagi survive, traces of the medieval church hidden beneath the Baroque stucco.
places.look: Look at the lunette above the portal: a mosaic beneath the great rose window.
places.aliases: Basilica di San Marco | Basilica of San Marco | Basilika San Marco | Basilique San Marco | Basílica de San Marcos

places.name: Piazza Affari and Palazzo Mezzanotte
places.subtitle: Stock exchange square · since 1932
places.s30: You are in Piazza Affari, the financial heart of Milan. The imposing building in front of you is Palazzo Mezzanotte, home of the stock exchange. In the middle of the square a marble hand raises its middle finger: this is L.O.V.E., Maurizio Cattelan's provocative work.
places.m2: The building takes its name from its architect, Paolo Mezzanotte, and was built between 1929 and 1932 to house the Milan stock exchange. Its solemn facade, typical of those years, is decorated with sculptures by Leone Lodi and Geminiano Cibau. While digging the foundations, workers uncovered the remains of a Roman theatre, which are still preserved in the basement. In the middle of the square stands the sculpture everyone photographs. Maurizio Cattelan installed it in 2010: a huge hand in Carrara marble with every finger cut off except the middle one. The title is an acronym for the Italian words for Freedom, Hatred, Vengeance and Eternity. It was meant to be temporary, but the artist donated it to the city on condition that it stay right here, in front of the stock exchange, and so it has. Look closely at the hand: many see in it a Roman salute with broken fingers, a provocation that speaks both of finance and of the history of this building, born in the Fascist era.
places.look: Look at the marble hand in the square: only the middle finger is left standing.
places.aliases: Piazza Affari and Palazzo Mezzanotte | Piazza Affari e Palazzo Mezzanotte | Piazza Affari et palais Mezzanotte | Piazza Affari und Palazzo Mezzanotte | Piazza Affari y Palacio Mezzanotte

places.name: Piazza Cordusio and Via Dante
places.subtitle: Elliptical square · late 1800s
places.s30: You are in Piazza Cordusio, the elliptical square built in the late nineteenth century as a showcase for banks and insurance companies. From here Via Dante begins, the pedestrian street running straight towards Sforza Castle and its tower.
places.m2: The name Cordusio comes from curtis ducis, the duke's court: in the early Middle Ages the Lombard dukes had their residence here. The square as you see it today, however, is the child of the great late nineteenth century makeover, when the city centre was redesigned and monumental buildings rose here for banks, insurers and the old stock exchange, before it moved to Piazza Affari. In the middle stands the monument to the poet Giuseppe Parini, by the sculptor Luigi Secchi. Via Dante was opened in those same years to link the heart of the city to the castle, and it works like a telescope. Stand at the start of the street and look to the end: the Filarete Tower, rebuilt by Luca Beltrami in the early twentieth century, closes the view perfectly. Along the way you will notice the elegant facades of the late nineteenth century buildings, with shops on the ground floor and middle class apartments above. Today it is pedestrian and one of the Milanese's favourite strolls, all the way to Largo Cairoli and the castle gates.
places.look: Look down Via Dante: the Filarete Tower closes the view at the far end.
places.aliases: Piazza Cordusio and Via Dante | Piazza Cordusio e via Dante | Piazza Cordusio et via Dante | Piazza Cordusio und Via Dante | Piazza Cordusio y Via Dante

places.name: Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio
places.subtitle: Romanesque basilica · from the 4th century
places.s30: In front of you stands the basilica founded by Ambrose, bishop and patron saint of Milan, at the end of the fourth century. What you see is the model of Lombard Romanesque, with its arcaded courtyard, gabled front and two bell towers from different ages.
places.m2: Ambrose consecrated it in 386 as the basilica of the martyrs, to hold the remains of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, and he chose to be buried here: he still lies in the crypt beside them. The building you see dates mostly from the eleventh and twelfth centuries, when it was rebuilt in Romanesque style. Before going in you cross the large arcaded courtyard, where people not yet baptised once had to wait. Now look up at the two bell towers. The lower, older one on the right belonged to the monks; the one on the left, begun in 1144, to the canons. The two communities quarrelled over the basilica for centuries. Inside is one of the great treasures of Milan, the golden altar made by Wolvinius in the ninth century, and next to the church there is a small museum. A curious detail: in the square, to the left of the basilica, stands a Roman column with two holes. Legend says they were left by the devil, whose horns got stuck there during a fight with Ambrose.
places.look: Look at the two bell towers: the low one of the monks, the tall one of the canons.
places.aliases: Basilica di Sant'Ambrogio | Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio | Basilika Sant'Ambrogio | Basilique Saint-Ambroise | Basílica de San Ambrosio

places.name: Santa Maria delle Grazie and the Last Supper
places.subtitle: Renaissance church · Leonardo's Last Supper
places.s30: In front of you is the Dominican church of Santa Maria delle Grazie, with its great rounded east end attributed to Bramante. In the refectory of the convent next door Leonardo painted the Last Supper, one of the most famous paintings in the world. Visits are by booking only.
places.m2: The church was begun in 1463 for the Dominican friars, designed by Guiniforte Solari in a style that was still Gothic. A few years later Ludovico Sforza, known as il Moro, decided to make it his family mausoleum and had the east end rebuilt in Renaissance style: that is the great domed structure you see dominating the square. His wife, Beatrice d'Este, was buried here in 1497. In the last years of the fifteenth century Leonardo painted the Last Supper on the refectory wall, using an experimental dry technique that proved fragile: the painting began to decay within a few decades. A true story: in August 1943 a bomb destroyed most of the refectory, yet the wall with the Last Supper, shielded by sandbags, survived. The last major restoration took more than twenty years and ended in 1999. Since 1980 the church and the Last Supper have been a Unesco World Heritage Site. Remember that the Last Supper can only be visited by booking, while the church is visited separately.
places.look: Look at Bramante's east end: the great brick drum crowning the church.
places.aliases: Santa Maria delle Grazie and the Last Supper | Santa Maria delle Grazie e il Cenacolo | Santa Maria delle Grazie et la Cène | Santa Maria delle Grazie und das Abendmahl | Santa Maria delle Grazie y la Última Cena

places.itwiki: Chiesa di San Maurizio al Monastero Maggiore
places.name: San Maurizio al Monastero Maggiore
places.subtitle: Renaissance church · from 1503
places.s30: In front of you is San Maurizio, the church of the Monastero Maggiore, once the most important convent for women in Milan. The front is plain, but inside almost every wall is covered with sixteenth century frescoes, which is why people call it the Sistine Chapel of Milan.
places.m2: The convent of Benedictine nuns had very ancient origins, and the church you see was begun in 1503. Inside, a wall splits the space in two: in front, the hall for the public; behind, the choir reserved for the cloistered nuns, who followed mass without being seen. The walls were frescoed by Bernardino Luini, one of the great Lombard painters of the Renaissance, by his sons and by other artists of his circle. The nuns' choir still holds an organ built by Giovan Giacomo Antegnati in 1554, which still works today. A curious detail: one of the frescoes in the nuns' hall shows Noah's Ark, and among the animals going aboard there are two unicorns. While you are out here, notice how simple the stone front is: it was meant not to draw attention, while all the richness stayed inside. The old convent buildings behind the church now house the Civic Archaeological Museum, where you can also see a tower from Milan's Roman walls.
places.look: Look at the plain front on Corso Magenta: it gives no hint of the frescoes inside.
places.aliases: San Maurizio al Monastero Maggiore

places.itwiki: Museo nazionale della scienza e della tecnologia Leonardo da Vinci
places.name: Leonardo da Vinci National Museum of Science and Technology
places.subtitle: Science museum · opened in 1953
places.s30: In front of you is the National Museum of Science and Technology, named after Leonardo da Vinci. It fills a sixteenth century monastery and is the largest museum of science and technology in Italy, with machines, trains, ships and even a submarine.
places.m2: The museum is housed in a monastery of the Olivetan monks, built in the sixteenth century next to the basilica of San Vittore al Corpo. After the damage of the Second World War, the engineer and industrialist Guido Ucelli had it restored and turned it into a museum, opened in 1953. The heart of the collection is the Leonardo gallery, with models of his machines built from the drawings in his notebooks. Then there are halls full of steam locomotives, aircraft, a large sailing ship and even parts of an ocean liner. A true story: the submarine Enrico Toti, the first built in Italy after the war, reached the museum in 2005, carried by road right across the city, and crowds of Milanese came out to watch. While you are out here, look for the bell tower of San Vittore: it shows how closely the museum is tied to this old religious complex, whose cloisters still survive. If you go in, take your time: you can easily spend hours here.
places.look: Look at the bell tower of San Vittore al Corpo: the museum is in its old monastery.
places.aliases: Leonardo da Vinci National Museum of Science and Technology | Museo Nacional de la Ciencia y la Tecnología Leonardo da Vinci | Museo Nazionale della Scienza e della Tecnologia Leonardo da Vinci | Musée national des Sciences et des Techniques Léonard de Vinci | Nationalmuseum für Wissenschaft und Technik Leonardo da Vinci

places.name: Columns of San Lorenzo
places.subtitle: Roman colonnade · 2nd to 3rd century
places.s30: In front of you stand sixteen Roman marble columns with Corinthian capitals. They are among the most important remains of Roman Milan, ancient Mediolanum, and for centuries they have formed a grand entrance to the basilica of San Lorenzo, which you can see behind them.
places.m2: The columns date from the second or third century after Christ and belonged to an older building, perhaps a temple or a bath house. When the basilica of San Lorenzo was built, between the late fourth and early fifth centuries, they were brought here and lined up to form the portico in front of the church. For centuries houses and workshops were built up against them, and they were only cleared away in the twentieth century. Step closer and look at the worn bases and capitals: they are almost two thousand years old. Between the columns and the basilica stands a bronze statue of the emperor Constantine, a copy of a Roman original, placed here in 1937. Constantine is tied to Milan because it was here, in 313, that Christians were granted freedom of worship, in what we know as the Edict of Milan. Today the churchyard is one of the liveliest spots in town, especially in the evening, when young people sit under the portico and on the steps.
places.look: Look at the bronze statue of Constantine between the columns and the basilica.
places.aliases: Colonne di San Lorenzo | Colonnes de San Lorenzo | Columnas de San Lorenzo | Columns of San Lorenzo | Säulen von San Lorenzo

places.name: Basilica of San Lorenzo Maggiore
places.subtitle: Early Christian basilica · 4th century
places.s30: In front of you is the basilica of San Lorenzo Maggiore, one of the oldest churches in Milan, built between the late fourth and early fifth centuries. Its central plan and great dome make it unlike any other church in the city.
places.m2: When it was built, Milan was one of the capitals of the Western Roman Empire, and the basilica was laid out on a central plan with four great apses and four towers at the corners. Over the centuries it suffered fires and collapses: the original dome fell in 1573 and was rebuilt by the architect Martino Bassi in the octagonal shape you still see today. The front facing the street is far more recent and dates from the late nineteenth century. Look up and find the towers flanking the dome: they are a reminder of the late Roman building. Inside, the chapel of Sant'Aquilino holds early Christian mosaics that are among the oldest in the city. A curious detail: behind the basilica lies the Parco delle Basiliche. This was once the Piazza della Vetra, where for centuries executions took place. Today it is a wide lawn linking San Lorenzo to Sant'Eustorgio, and crossing it is the nicest way to reach the next stop, strolling between two of the oldest churches in Milan.
places.look: Look at the great octagonal dome rising behind the front, between the towers.
places.aliases: Basilica di San Lorenzo Maggiore | Basilica of San Lorenzo Maggiore | Basilika San Lorenzo Maggiore | Basilique San Lorenzo Maggiore | Basílica de San Lorenzo Maggiore

places.name: Basilica of Sant'Eustorgio
places.subtitle: Basilica of the Magi · Romanesque and Gothic
places.s30: In front of you is the basilica of Sant'Eustorgio, bound up with the legend of the Three Kings, whose relics were kept here for centuries. Look at the bell tower: at the top there is no cross but a star, recalling the one that guided the Magi to Bethlehem.
places.m2: According to tradition, in the fourth century Bishop Eustorgius brought the relics of the Three Kings from Constantinople to Milan and built a church outside the walls to keep them. In 1164, after conquering the city, the emperor Frederick Barbarossa had them taken to Cologne, where they still lie in the cathedral. Only at the start of the twentieth century did a few fragments come back to Milan. The church was later entrusted to the Dominican friars and rebuilt several times, and the bell tower with the star went up between the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. Inside is the marble tomb of Saint Peter Martyr, carved by Giovanni di Balduccio, and behind the apse lies the Portinari Chapel, one of the masterpieces of the early Renaissance in Milan, with frescoes by Vincenzo Foppa. The cloisters and the chapel are now part of the Sant'Eustorgio Museum. A curious detail: every year on the sixth of January, the procession of the Three Kings sets off from the cathedral and ends right in front of this basilica, with music and costumes.
places.look: Look at the top of the bell tower: instead of a cross there is a star.
places.aliases: Basilica di Sant'Eustorgio | Basilica of Sant'Eustorgio | Basilika Sant'Eustorgio | Basilique Sant'Eustorgio | Basílica de Sant'Eustorgio

places.name: Darsena
places.subtitle: Milan's old harbour · shaped in 1603
places.s30: In front of you is the Darsena, Milan's old harbour, where boats laden with goods arrived along the canals. Since its restoration in 2015 it has become a broad square on the water, where the Milanese come to stroll and sit along the banks.
places.m2: Milan has no sea, yet for centuries it was an important port. This is where the Naviglio Grande and the Naviglio Pavese meet, the canals that linked the city to the river Ticino, to Lake Maggiore and to the Po. The basin took its present shape in 1603, under Spanish rule, right against the city walls. Boats brought sand, stone, timber and farm produce, and as late as the nineteen fifties the Darsena was still among the busiest Italian ports for goods. The last barge full of sand tied up here in 1979, and years of neglect followed. For Expo 2015 the Darsena was cleaned up and redesigned, with new walkways along the banks and a covered city market. During the works the Ticinello, an old canal buried for decades under Piazza Ventiquattro Maggio, was brought back to light. Now look east, towards the great neoclassical arch of Porta Ticinese: it marked the entrance to the city for anyone arriving from this side.
places.look: Look east: the neoclassical arch of Porta Ticinese closes off the Darsena.
places.aliases: Darsena

places.name: Naviglio Grande and Vicolo dei Lavandai
places.subtitle: Navigable canal · from 1177
places.s30: In front of you flows the Naviglio Grande, the oldest of Milan's canals, bringing water from the river Ticino right into the city. Along the bank opens the Vicolo dei Lavandai, with the old wash house where for centuries people scrubbed their laundry in canal water.
places.m2: Digging of the Naviglio Grande began in 1177, and by the thirteenth century the canal reached Milan: it is about fifty kilometres long and starts from the river Ticino. For centuries it was a true highway of water, and its boats even carried the Candoglia marble, quarried near Lake Maggiore, that was used to build the cathedral. Along the banks, where boatmen and craftsmen once lived, there are now bars, galleries and small shops. Now let your eyes wander into the Vicolo dei Lavandai. You will see a narrow channel with sloping stone slabs and a wooden roof: this is where laundry was washed with water and soap, rubbed hard against the stone. The wash house stayed in use until the middle of the twentieth century. The name means alley of the washermen, a reminder that this job was not only done by women. Today it is one of the most photographed corners of Milan, above all at sunset, when the lights of the houses are reflected in the water of the canal.
places.look: Look at the sloping stone slabs of the wash house: laundry was scrubbed there.
places.aliases: Naviglio Grande and Vicolo dei Lavandai | Naviglio Grande e Vicolo dei Lavandai | Naviglio Grande et Vicolo dei Lavandai | Naviglio Grande und Vicolo dei Lavandai | Naviglio Grande y Vicolo dei Lavandai

places.name: Monza Cathedral
places.subtitle: Theodelinda's basilica · Gothic from 1300
places.s30: In front of you stands Monza Cathedral, the church founded by the Lombard queen Theodelinda. Its facade of white and green marble bands dates from the fourteenth century, and inside it keeps one of the oldest symbols of Europe, the Iron Crown.
places.m2: The story begins at the end of the sixth century, when Queen Theodelinda had a chapel built here, dedicated to Saint John the Baptist. The church you see today was begun in 1300, and its striped facade is the work of Matteo da Campione. Look up at the great central rose window. Inside, in the north arm of the transept, is the Chapel of Theodelinda: forty-five scenes painted in the mid-fifteenth century by the Zavattari family tell the queen's life, and they are a masterpiece of International Gothic painting in Italy. The altar of this chapel holds the Iron Crown. According to tradition, the thin band of iron inside it was hammered from a nail of the cross of Christ. Kings of Italy were crowned with it, and in 1805 Napoleon placed it on his own head in Milan Cathedral. Next to the church, the Cathedral Museum and Treasury keeps the gifts linked to Theodelinda, including the famous gilded silver hen with her chicks.
places.look: Look at the great rose window set among the white and green marble bands.
places.aliases: Catedral de Monza | Cathédrale de Monza | Dom von Monza | Duomo di Monza | Monza Cathedral

places.name: Arengario
places.subtitle: Medieval town hall · late 1200s
places.s30: This building raised on stone arches is the Arengario, the old town hall of Monza, built at the end of the thirteenth century. Citizens gathered here, and from here the commune spoke to the town, just a few steps from the cathedral, almost challenging it.
places.m2: The name comes from the medieval Latin arengarius, from a Germanic word for the place of assembly. We are at the end of the thirteenth century, the age of the free communes, and Monza builds its public palace right next to the cathedral, so that civic and religious power stand face to face. On the ground floor is the great portico held up by massive stone pillars, where people met to talk and trade. Above, a single hall under a timber roof hosted the assemblies. Now look for the small balcony jutting out from the facade: it is called the parlera, and from there the decrees and decisions of the commune were read aloud to the citizens gathered in the square. Then raise your eyes to the bell tower on the north side, added later: at the top it has swallowtail battlements, the kind known as Ghibelline. Beside it once stood the palace of the podestà, linked by a raised walkway, but it vanished long ago. Today the upper hall often hosts temporary exhibitions.
places.look: Look at the small balcony on the facade: the parlera, where decrees were read out.
places.aliases: Arengario

places.name: Piazza Roma and Piazza Trento e Trieste
places.subtitle: Civic squares · war memorial, 1932
places.s30: You are in the civic heart of Monza. Piazza Roma, with the Arengario, opens onto the nearby Piazza Trento e Trieste, dominated by the Town Hall and by the great memorial to the fallen of the First World War. For centuries the town has gathered here.
places.m2: Piazza Trento e Trieste has a long past. It was once a large meadow, called Pratum Magnum in Latin, and since the Middle Ages it hosted the market and the fair of Saint John, the patron saint of the town. Its present name recalls Trento and Trieste, the two cities that became Italian at the end of the First World War. On the north side you see the Town Hall, from 1932. In the middle rises the war memorial by the sculptor Enrico Pancera, made between 1922 and 1932: on a base of pinkish stone, a bronze group of soldiers advances, led by Victory. Later, the names of people from Monza who died in the wars that followed were added too. Between 2005 and 2009 the square was redesigned with nods to its history: the water channels recall the old Pelucca canal, and some paving tiles carry the marks of fifteenth-century merchants. A few steps away, Piazza Roma is the cosier living room around the Arengario, where locals have met for generations.
places.look: Look at the war memorial: bronze soldiers advance, led by the figure of Victory.
places.aliases: Piazza Roma and Piazza Trento e Trieste | Piazza Roma e Piazza Trento e Trieste | Piazza Roma et Piazza Trento e Trieste | Piazza Roma und Piazza Trento e Trieste | Piazza Roma y Piazza Trento e Trieste

places.name: Bridge of the Lions
places.subtitle: Bridge over the Lambro · 1842
places.s30: This is the Bridge of the Lions, over the river Lambro. You will recognise it by the four marble lions guarding its corners. It dates from 1842, but right beside it hides a much older story: the remains of a bridge from Roman times.
places.m2: The bridge was built in 1842, when the new road then called Via Ferdinandea was opened, today Via Vittorio Emanuele the Second. It has three arches resting on granite abutments, and the four marble lions, one at each corner, have become one of the best loved symbols of Monza. Yet this point on the Lambro was an important crossing long before. The modern bridge stands on the remains of the old Roman bridge known as the Arena bridge. Look towards one of the two ends: an arch of the Roman structure is still visible, a small window onto two thousand years of the town's history. From the bridge two walks run along the river, towards the areas where grain mills once turned, irrigation channels flowed through the fields and women came to the wash houses. Look around you: a few old tenement houses with long shared balconies still tell the story of working Monza living beside the water. The Lambro rises between the two arms of Lake Como and flows all the way to the Po.
places.look: Look at the corners of the bridge: four marble lions keep watch over the Lambro.
places.aliases: Bridge of the Lions | Löwenbrücke | Pont des Lions | Ponte dei Leoni | Puente de los Leones

places.itwiki: Chiesa di Santa Maria in Strada (Monza)
places.name: Santa Maria in Strada
places.subtitle: Gothic brick church · 1348 to 1368
places.s30: In front of you is Santa Maria in Strada, with one of the finest Gothic terracotta facades in Lombardy. The name comes from the road that linked Monza to Milan, along which the church was built in the mid-fourteenth century.
places.m2: The church was built between 1348 and 1368 at the wish of a community of Franciscan tertiaries, and at the end of the century it passed to the Augustinians. Look at the facade: it is a small treatise on Lombard Gothic, with its false loggia and rich terracotta decoration, inspired by the cathedral facade and by Pisan sculpture. In the centre is the rose window, flanked by two pointed windows, and at the top, between two roundels, stands a statue of the Madonna and Child. What you see is a copy: the stone original, from the early fifteenth century, was removed in 1995 to protect it. Notice the figure's prominent belt: it may be a tribute to the Augustinian devotion to Our Lady of the Girdle. Two frescoes of the Annunciation once flanked the doorway, and they are now kept in the Cathedral Museum and Treasury. The interior was remodelled in the eighteenth century, while the facade was restored in 1870 to a design by Carlo Maciachini. Beside the church hides a small, recently restored cloister.
places.look: Look at the top of the facade: the Madonna and Child standing between two roundels.
places.aliases: Chiesa di Santa Maria in Strada | Iglesia de Santa Maria in Strada | Kirche Santa Maria in Strada | Santa Maria in Strada | Église Santa Maria in Strada

places.name: Royal Villa of Monza
places.subtitle: Neoclassical palace · 1777 to 1780
places.s30: Before you opens the Royal Villa, built at the end of the eighteenth century by Giuseppe Piermarini, the architect of La Scala, for Archduke Ferdinand of Habsburg. It was home to viceroys and kings, and today it is a museum facing one of the largest parks in Europe.
places.m2: Work took place between 1777 and 1780: Empress Maria Theresa of Austria wanted a summer residence for her son Ferdinand, governor of Milan. Piermarini designed a neoclassical palace shaped like a U, with a central block and two long wings embracing the main courtyard. In Napoleonic times the viceroy Eugène de Beauharnais lived here, and after Italian unification the villa became one of the favourite homes of the House of Savoy. Everything changed on 29 July 1900, when King Umberto the First was killed in Monza by the anarchist Gaetano Bresci. His son, Victor Emmanuel the Third, no longer wished to live here, and the villa lost its role as a royal palace. Today you can visit the royal apartments inside, as well as the Rotunda painted by Andrea Appiani with the story of Cupid and Psyche. Behind the palace stretch the royal gardens, with a small lake, a neoclassical temple and the rose garden named after Niso Fumagalli, a real show in spring. The villa shines again after the major restoration that reopened it to the public in 2014.
places.look: Look how the two wings of the villa reach out to embrace the main courtyard.
places.aliases: Königliche Villa Monza | Royal Villa of Monza | Villa Real de Monza | Villa Reale di Monza | Villa royale de Monza

places.name: Monza Park
places.subtitle: Napoleonic walled park · since 1805
places.s30: You are in Monza Park, one of the largest walled parks in Europe: about seven hundred hectares of meadows, woods, farmsteads and villas, enclosed by a wall more than fourteen kilometres long. The Lambro runs through it, and inside there is even a racing circuit.
places.m2: The park was created in 1805 by Napoleonic decree, and work began the following year. The story goes that Josephine Bonaparte asked her son Eugène de Beauharnais, viceroy of Italy, for a park larger than the one at Versailles. The design was entrusted to Luigi Canonica, a pupil of Piermarini, who did not erase the existing countryside but absorbed it: villas, farmsteads, mills and roads all became part of the plan. That is why, as you walk, you come across real farms such as Cascina Frutteto or Cascina Cernuschi, and old mills along the Lambro, among them the Mulino del Cantone. Look out too for Villa Mirabello, a house older than the park itself, which grew up around it, and nearby the smaller Villa Mirabellino. The park has several souls: the royal gardens near the Royal Villa, the wide meadows and woods along the river, and further north the racing circuit. Today it is the great green lung of Brianza, and at weekends it fills with families, runners and cyclists along its long tree-lined avenues.
places.look: Look at the long tree-lined avenues: they still follow the nineteenth-century plan.
places.aliases: Monza Park | Parc de Monza | Parco di Monza | Park von Monza | Parque de Monza

places.name: Monza Circuit
places.subtitle: The Temple of Speed · since 1922
places.s30: You are at the Monza Circuit, the Temple of Speed. In front of the pits runs the main straight, where Formula One cars reach some of the highest speeds of the whole championship. The Italian Grand Prix has been raced here since 1922.
places.m2: The Automobile Club of Milan decided to build the circuit at the start of 1922 to celebrate its twenty-fifth anniversary. Work began on 15 May, and about three thousand five hundred workers finished the track in just over a hundred days. It opened on 3 September 1922, and on 10 September the second Italian Grand Prix was raced here. Since then the Grand Prix has been held here almost every year: since 1950 the only exception was 1980, when the track was being rebuilt. In the 1950s the high-speed oval was added, with banked curves tilted at about thirty degrees, home to races between European and American drivers nicknamed Monzanapolis. The last race on the banking was in 1969, but those restored concrete walls still stand among the trees. Today's circuit is just under six kilometres long. Look around you: the grandstands, the pits and the podium hanging over the straight are the stage of a unique tradition, the fans who flood onto the track at the end of the race in a sea of red.
places.look: Look at the podium hanging over the straight: after the race the crowd floods the track.
places.aliases: Autodromo Nazionale Monza | Autodromo Nazionale di Monza | Circuit de Monza | Circuito de Monza | Monza Circuit
